mcqs.question: Why does building an accessible custom combobox require more work than building an accessible custom checkbox?
options: It doesn't — both require the identical amount of ARIA and keyboard work
A combobox has no valid ARIA role at all, unlike a checkbox

A combobox involves multiple coordinated interactive parts (input, popup listbox, individual options) whose ARIA state must stay correlated, while a checkbox is a single element with one state to track
A checkbox requires more testing because it has more possible visual states
mcqs.explanation: A combobox coordinates several elements — the text input, the popup listbox, and each option — all of which need synchronized, correct ARIA state, which is a genuinely larger surface than a single checkbox's one boolean state. Comboboxes do have valid ARIA roles, and checkboxes don't inherently require more visual-state testing than a well-scoped combobox implementation.

mcqs.question: A custom modal uses `aria-labelledby="modal-title"` pointing at its own visible `<h2>` heading, rather than a separate `aria-label` string with the same text. Why is this the preferred choice?
options: aria-label is not supported on dialog roles at all
aria-labelledby is required by the HTML spec for any element with role="dialog"
It has no real advantage — both approaches are functionally and practically identical
It avoids duplicating the same text in two places that could independently drift out of sync if the heading is edited later
mcqs.explanation: Pointing aria-labelledby at the existing visible heading means there's a single source of truth for the dialog's name — editing the heading automatically updates the accessible name too, whereas a separate aria-label string has to be manually kept in sync and can silently drift. aria-label is fully valid on dialog roles and there's no such HTML-spec requirement mandating aria-labelledby specifically.

mcqs.question: In a combobox implementation, why does `aria-activedescendant` update on the text input rather than moving real DOM focus into the listbox as the user presses arrow keys?
options: So the browser can render the listbox with better performance
So real keyboard focus stays in the text input, letting the user keep typing to refine their search while browsing highlighted options
Because listbox elements cannot receive DOM focus under any circumstances
Because aria-activedescendant is required to be on the input element by the HTML specification
mcqs.explanation: Keeping real DOM focus on the input while aria-activedescendant tracks the highlighted option lets the user continue typing to filter results while still navigating suggestions with arrow keys — moving actual focus into the listbox would break that ability to keep typing. This isn't a rendering-performance technique, listbox elements can receive focus in other patterns, and there's no such focus-location mandate in the HTML spec.

mcqs.question: In a tab interface using the roving-tabindex pattern, what should happen to `tabindex` values when the user moves from Tab 1 to Tab 3 using the arrow keys?
options: All tabs update to tabindex="0" simultaneously
Nothing changes — roving tabindex only applies to mouse interaction
Every tab keeps tabindex="-1" permanently; only aria-selected changes
Tab 1's tabindex flips from "0" to "-1", and Tab 3's flips from "-1" to "0", so exactly one tab remains in the natural Tab-key sequence at all times
mcqs.explanation: Roving tabindex maintains exactly one tabindex="0" at a time, moving it to whichever tab currently has focus so a subsequent Tab key press exits the tab list at the right point rather than cycling through every tab individually. It's specifically a keyboard-navigation pattern (not mouse-only), and both tabindex and aria-selected need to update together, not just one of them.

mcqs.question: A tab component has correct `role="tab"`/`"tabpanel"` markup but is missing the `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` pairing between each tab and its panel. What's the practical consequence?
options: The tabs stop being keyboard-operable entirely
The component becomes completely invisible to screen readers
The tab set remains functionally usable, but a screen reader user loses the explicit "this tab shows this panel" relationship and must infer it from context
The panels will fail to hide/show correctly when switching tabs
mcqs.explanation: The aria-controls/aria-labelledby pairing is what makes the tab-to-panel relationship explicit for assistive tech; without it the component still functions and remains visible, but that specific relationship has to be inferred rather than announced directly. Keyboard operability, screen reader visibility, and panel show/hide behavior are all separate concerns unaffected by this particular omission.

mcqs.question: A team builds a custom dropdown menu with valid ARIA roles but invents their own keyboard scheme (Tab instead of arrow keys to move between items) instead of checking the APG's menu pattern first. What's the specific problem with this, beyond it just being untested?
options: It violates the accessible name computation algorithm
It breaks screen reader users' learned expectations built from every other menu that follows the established pattern, even though the ARIA markup itself may be technically valid
ARIA roles are only valid when paired with the APG's exact keyboard scheme, so the roles themselves become invalid
It has no real downside as long as the roles and states are correct
mcqs.explanation: The subtler failure here is a convention mismatch, not a markup error — screen reader users build cross-site muscle memory around standard interaction patterns, and a menu that diverges from it forces relearning for no real benefit, even while its roles and states remain technically valid. This has nothing to do with accessible-name computation, and ARIA role validity doesn't depend on matching any specific keyboard scheme.
